briefFidelity: FAIL, and this is the gate. The brief asks for sediment as PURE PATTERN, a core sample with 'no single element dominating', filling the frame edge to edge, explicitly not a landscape. Blind, before reading a word of it, I wrote that the work is 'an object caught behind a shutter' and that the amber shard cluster 'is always the focal mass' and 'the only saturated colour in the work'. That is a figure-and-ground composition, which is the one reading the brief rules out, and I arrived at it without being able to be anchored. The bedding is not the subject in most of the set: 9548, 10264 and 10085 are amber starbursts with only a light wash of bars across them; 9190 and 10980 are thrown sticks with a few slats; 10801 has almost no bars at all and is a small knot ringed by dark discs. Only 9906, 10443 and 10622 read as a section - 3 of 12. The frame requirement fails alongside it: 9011, 9369, 10801 and the 512 single put a small centred patch of slats in a large empty black field, and that empty field above and below functions as exactly the sky and ground plane the brief forbids. The bar lengths also taper symmetrically about a centre line, which builds a lens or a barcode, not a bed - deposition has no reason to be bilaterally symmetric. Finally the brief names 'a cold slate band' as a palette member; blind I recorded 'no second hue anywhere', and measuring the sheets confirms it - 100% of drawn pixels fall in hue 20-45 degrees, 0.0000% anywhere cool. The commissioned work is a stratigraphic section; the delivered work is an emblem with banding over it.
composition: There is a clear focal hierarchy and it is well made - which is the problem, because the brief asked for none. The saturated amber mass dominates every seed and the eye goes to it before it goes to any band: 9548 and 10264 are entirely about the starburst, 9011 and 9369 about a small heraldic arrowhead. Everything is centred and symmetric about a vertical axis, so the frame is addressed as a stage rather than as a crop through a continuous body. The frame is genuinely used in only 9906, 10443 and 10622, where slats run off both edges; in 9011, 9369, 10801, 9190 and the 512 single the work floats in the middle with wide empty margins on all four sides. As an independent picture 9906 is the best composition in the set. As an answer to this brief the hierarchy is inverted.
collectionCoherence: Strong, and the clearest pass on any axis. All twelve share one ground, one warm palette family, one three-layer grammar (dark dots, over-printing horizontal slats, amber shards) and one hard-edged flat drawing language with no strokes or outlines. Laid out together they are unmistakably one project: 9011 and 9906 look nothing alike in density yet obviously came from the same hand. 10801 is the one member that strains the set - large regular discs, almost no bedding - and reads closer to a different series, but it still sits inside the palette and the centred layout. This is a collection, not a folder.
palette: Chosen, controlled, and one member short. The warm earth family is real - umber, ochre, sand and khaki over a near-black base - and the ground genuinely supports the drawing: the amber pops hard against it and the pale slats sit at a believable mid value. But the brief names four things and delivers three: the 'cold slate band' is absent, and not merely muted. Every drawn pixel across both 256 sheets measures in a single warm wedge of hue 20-45 degrees with zero cool pixels; what looks slate in 9906, 10443 and 10622 is a warm grey-olive at hue 40. That missing cold note is not cosmetic - it is the one value that would have separated one bed from the next by MATERIAL rather than by width, which is exactly what the brief asked the palette to do. Contrast range is doing work in 9906 and 10622 and is doing very little in 10801, whose discs are so close to the ground they barely register.
seedVariation: Genuinely wide and well judged, and it delivers the brief's own stated axis - tokens do differ in how many beds they carry and how evenly they are spaced. Four registers are legible: bar-dominant (9906, 10443, 10622), shard-dominant (9548, 10264, 10085), compact-in-a-void (9011, 9369, 10801) and sparse sticks (9190, 10980). These are twelve different works, not one work at twelve rotations, and the spread does not break the project - only 10801 pulls at the edges of it. The reservation is that much of the variety is carried by the shard layer, which the brief never commissioned; if you removed it, 9548, 10264, 10085 and 9190 would collapse toward each other and the true bedding variation would be much narrower than this sheet suggests.
thumbnailSurvival: Mixed, and it fails on the brief's own wording. At 120 the amber silhouette survives completely - 9011, 9548, 10264 and 10801 are instantly told apart - and the twelve do still read as twelve things, separating mainly by density and by bar-to-amber ratio. But the bands stop being individual beds and become a haze: the brief asks that weight and thickness differ 'so the eye reads a sequence rather than a texture', and at browse size 9727, 9906, 10085 and 10980 all read as texture, converging into one impression of an amber tangle inside a horizontal smear. The dot layer is simply gone at 120 in every seed except 10801 and, faintly, 9190 and 10264 - a whole layer that renders and does not read at the size the collection is actually seen.
marketResponse: Visible, consistently directed, and half inverted. The change is carried almost entirely by the band layer and it is legible at 120 for 9011 and 9369, subtler for 9190, and weakest for 9548, whose three states are all a dense amber mass separated only by internal texture. The count direction matches the brief exactly: fewer beds survive under stress (9369 stress loses most of its stack and most of its bottom dot arc) and more return in recovery (9369 recovery regains a full top and bottom arc). The thickness direction runs the other way. The brief says beds should THIN under drawdown and the sequence should THICKEN in recovery; what is on the sheet is that stress leaves the FEW THICKEST, most opaque slabs in the entire set (9011 stress, 9369 stress) while recovery is many fine pale lines (9011 recovery). Read as 'thin out to fewer' the wording is satisfied; read as per-bed thickness it is delivered backwards, and the stress rows read as a shutter opening rather than as a sequence being eroded.
tokenIdentity: Strong and not in question. Across all three states 9011 keeps its downward amber arrowhead, 9190 its crossed scaffold of long sticks, 9369 its compact body and 9548 its starburst; nothing becomes a different object under drawdown. What changes is band count, pitch, weight and overall luminance, plus a small re-angling and spread of the shards in 9548 and 9190 that never crosses into a new subject. If anything identity is held a little too firmly in 9548, where the state rows are nearly interchangeable at 120.
artifacts: Nothing reads as a rendering failure, but there are real defects. Bands are cut by the viewBox at both left and right edges in 9906, 10443 and 10622 - defensible as bleed for a core sample, except that 10443's bottom-most pale band is a full-width slab that hits both edges and flattens the bottom of the frame into a bar. Dots are clipped mid-circle at the frame edge in 9011 lower left and 9727 left, which reads as an accident rather than a crop. Where three or four band values interleave in 9906 and 10622 the overlap produces a moire that competes with the sequence it is meant to build. And the dot layer in 9011, 9369, 9727 and 10443 sits so close to the ground in value that it is invisible at 120 and nearly invisible at 256 - present in the bytes, absent to the viewer.
reasoning: The gate decides this and nothing else needed to. I described these sheets before reading a single line of the brief, and what I wrote was that the work is an object seen behind a shutter, with a saturated amber cluster that 'is always the focal mass', floating centred in a large empty black field, and with 'no second hue anywhere'. The brief then turned out to ask for sediment as pure pattern, a core sample rather than a landscape, filling the frame edge to edge with no single element dominating, in a palette that includes a cold slate band. Three of its central requirements are contradicted by my own blind reading - dominance, frame use, and the missing cool note - and the contradiction is not marginal: in half the set (9548, 10264, 10085, 9190, 10801) the bedding is subordinate scenery behind a figure, and only 9906, 10443 and 10622 read as a section at all. This is accomplished work with real collection coherence, genuine seed variation and a legible market response, and it would deserve a serious look against a brief about an emblem behind interference. It is not the thing that was commissioned, and the brief is explicit enough that this cannot be read as interpretation. Committing it permanently would commit the wrong artwork.
wouldChange: Demote or delete the amber shard cluster. It is the best-drawn thing here and it is the reason the work fails; at most it should become one anomalous bed among beds - a slumped or intruded layer inside the sequence - never a centred figure with margin around it. Run the beds truly edge to edge in every seed, top to bottom, and remove the symmetric taper of band lengths about the centre line so the frame reads as a crop through a continuous body rather than as a stage holding a lens; 9906 already shows this working and should be the floor for the set, not its maximum. Introduce the cold slate band as an actual cool hue rather than a warm grey - one genuinely blue-grey bed per token would let the eye read material change and turn the texture back into a sequence at 120px. Invert the per-bed thickness response so drawdown leaves thin, starved beds and recovery deposits thick ones, which is both what the brief says and the more legible reading of erosion. Finally either raise the dot layer's value until it survives at 120 or cut it, and fix the mid-circle dot clipping in 9011 and 9727 and the full-width bottom slab in 10443.
